name: Callback digits, typical after-hours line
rationale: This is most of your traffic and one wrong digit means you dial a stranger back instead of a patient waiting on a callback.

name: Self-corrected callback number under noise
rationale: Callers routinely fumble a digit and fix it, and a vendor that keeps the first number sends your night staff to a dead line.
channel_desc: typical after-hours call: background babble ~9 dB SNR, G.711, packet loss

name: Code-switched prescription plus number, worst-case line
rationale: Your hardest real calls — a shouted discharge instruction in a noisy room — are where a wrong dose or a garbled number becomes a safety incident.
channel_desc: worst realistic case: 4 dB SNR, heavy dropouts, reverberant room

rationale: If a vendor misses drug names and numbers even on a clean pharmacy call, it is broadly unfit and you can stop evaluating it here.
channel_desc: quiet room, cell phone, mild codec — the easy end of your traffic

name: Heavy code-switch symptom and dose, no phone number
rationale: These get read by a triage nurse rather than dialled, so errors cost you time and clarification calls but not a misdial.

**96% confidence** it is the best of 6 candidates for *your* traffic. The exam cost **$0.08** and 20 probes (118 probes saved by stopping early).

- **Callback digits, typical after-hours line** (weight 28%): 0% error — This is most of your traffic and one wrong digit means you dial a stranger back instead of a patient waiting on a callback.
- **Self-corrected callback number under noise** (weight 22%): 0% error — Callers routinely fumble a digit and fix it, and a vendor that keeps the first number sends your night staff to a dead line.
- **Code-switched prescription plus number, worst-case line** (weight 30%): 0% error — Your hardest real calls — a shouted discharge instruction in a noisy room — are where a wrong dose or a garbled number becomes a safety incident.
